tryit.networkFailHelp: The line above is the browser's raw error; for security, browsers hide the exact cause from scripts. Typical causes: CORS blocking (missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin for this origin), DNS or TLS failure, no network, or a request blocked by an extension. The devtools Network tab shows the precise reason.
tryit.corsProxyHint: A CORS proxy is configured: enable “Route through CORS proxy” and retry.
tryit.insights.followTitle: Sends the stored request again against the URL the server gave — not what the form currently holds.
tryit.insights.conditionalReplayTitle: Sends the stored request again with its validator: a 304 with no body proves the API honours conditional requests.
tryit.insights.fromCacheTitle: Served by the browser's cache: the duration next to it timed a local read, not a round trip.
tryit.diag.note: Diagnosis inferred from a test request sent after the failure; the devtools Network tab shows the exact reason.
tryit.diag.offlineHint: The browser reports being offline. Check your connection — nothing here points at a problem with the API.
tryit.diag.mixedContent: Most likely: blocked as mixed content.
tryit.diag.mixedContentHint: This page is served over https and the request targets http; browsers block that outright. Use an https server URL, or route the call through a CORS proxy.
tryit.diag.corsHint: The server answered a test request, so it is reachable — it just doesn't allow this origin. The API has to send Access-Control-Allow-Origin for this page, or the call has to go through a proxy.
tryit.diag.corsHintProxyOff: The server answered a test request, so it is reachable — it just doesn't allow this origin. A CORS proxy is configured: enable “Route through CORS proxy” and retry.
tryit.diag.corsProxied: Most likely: the proxy blocked the call.
tryit.diag.corsProxiedHint: The call went through the CORS proxy, which answered without the CORS headers the browser needs. That is the proxy's configuration to fix, not the API's.
tryit.diag.unreachable: Most likely: the server is unreachable.
tryit.diag.unreachableHint: A test request got no answer at all — DNS, TLS, or the server itself. Check the URL, and that the server is up.
tryit.exposeNote: Every header the browser exposes is listed here, unfiltered. On cross-origin calls the browser itself hides all other headers unless the API sends Access-Control-Expose-Headers (Set-Cookie is never readable from scripts) — the devtools Network tab shows the full raw list.

audit.title: Schema audit
audit.settings.hint: Analyzes the OpenAPI schema behind this documentation and reports what is wrong or missing, scored by category.
audit.intro: What this schema looks like to the tools that read it, this documentation included. Everything is computed in your browser — nothing is sent anywhere.
audit.disabled: The schema audit is disabled on this documentation.
audit.specOverlaid: This audit grades the schema with {count} OpenAPI overlay(s) this documentation applies; the download is the published file, without them.
audit.specOverlaidUser: This audit grades the schema with {count} OpenAPI overlay(s) applied, your own local patch included; the download is the published file, without them.
audit.help.title: How to read this report
audit.help.scoring: Each category scores the weighted pass rate of the checks that apply to this schema — an error weighs three times a note. A check that does not apply is not counted, so an API that deprecates nothing scores 100 % on deprecation rather than 0. The overall grade comes from the mean of the category scores.
audit.help.severity.error: Almost certainly a bug in the schema: the document contradicts itself, or contradicts the OpenAPI specification.
audit.help.severity.warning: Not invalid, but it costs the people reading these docs or generating a client from them.
audit.help.severity.info: Worth knowing, and worth a deliberate decision — not something you necessarily have to change.
audit.help.category.correctness: What is wrong: duplicate identifiers, parameters that go nowhere, examples their own schema rejects, constructs that contradict the declared OpenAPI version.
audit.help.category.completeness: What is missing: operations, parameters, properties and request bodies with no description, responses with no example, an info block with nothing in it.
audit.help.category.deprecation: The inventory of everything marked deprecated, and whether each one says what to use instead or when it goes away.
audit.help.category.consistency: Whether the document keeps to its own conventions: naming of parameters, of properties and of path segments, and shapes written out inline instead of shared.
audit.help.category.readiness: What this documentation cannot do with this schema: unstable deep links, ungrouped operations, no environment to seed, no OAuth flow to run, prefilled requests generated for lack of examples.
audit.empty.title: No findings.
audit.empty.hint: Every applicable check passes on this schema.
audit.rule.duplicate-operation-id.label: Duplicate operationId
audit.rule.duplicate-operation-id.messag: operationId “{operationId}” is used by more than one operation.
audit.rule.duplicate-operation-id.why: An operationId must be unique in the document, and this documentation turns it into the operation's deep link: one of the two links lands on the other operation. Rename one of them.
audit.rule.path-param-declared.label: Path placeholder with no parameter
audit.rule.path-param-declared.message: The path uses “{name}”, which no parameter declares.
audit.rule.path-param-declared.why: The reader gets no field to fill it in, and the try-it sends the unfilled placeholder as part of the URL. Declare a parameter named {name} with in: path.
audit.rule.path-param-in-template.label: Path parameter absent from the path
audit.rule.path-param-in-template.messag: The path parameter “{name}” appears nowhere in the path.
audit.rule.path-param-in-template.why: It is rendered as a required field that goes nowhere — usually a rename that stopped halfway. Fix the path, or drop the parameter.
audit.rule.path-param-required.label: Path parameter not marked required
audit.rule.path-param-required.message: The path parameter “{name}” is not marked required.
audit.rule.path-param-required.why: The OpenAPI specification makes required: true mandatory on a path parameter. This app forces it anyway, but code generators and validators are entitled to reject the document.
audit.rule.required-property-declared.la: Required property that is not declared
audit.rule.required-property-declared.me: “{name}” is listed in required but is not among the properties.
audit.rule.required-property-declared.wh: The field is mandatory yet described nowhere, so the try-it form cannot even offer it. Describe it in properties, or drop it from required.
audit.rule.required-with-default.label: Required, and still carrying a default
audit.rule.required-with-default.message: “{name}” is required and still declares a default.
audit.rule.required-with-default.why: A value the caller must always supply never falls back to anything, so the default can never apply — and it says the opposite of required. Readers and code generators get contradictory signals about whether the field has to be sent. Drop the default, or make the field optional.
audit.rule.example-type-mismatch.label: Example contradicting its schema
audit.rule.example-type-mismatch.message: The example {value} contradicts the schema it illustrates.
audit.rule.example-type-mismatch.why: Readers copy examples and the try-it prefills requests with them, so a wrong one spreads into every client. Align the value with the declared type or enum.
audit.rule.default-allowed.label: Default rejected by its own schema
audit.rule.default-allowed.message: The default {value} is rejected by its own schema.
audit.rule.default-allowed.why: The form prefills a value the API will refuse, and generators copy it as-is. Bring the default back inside the declared enum or range.
audit.rule.unused-component.label: Component never referenced
audit.rule.unused-component.why: A dead component documents nothing, yet it is downloaded by every reader and still has to be maintained. Delete it, or reference it where it belongs.
audit.rule.security-scheme-declared.labe: Security requirement on an undefined scheme
audit.rule.security-scheme-declared.mess: The security requirement names “{name}”, which components.securitySchemes does not define.
audit.rule.security-scheme-declared.why: The operation looks protected, but there is no scheme to build a credentials form from and no credentials are ever sent. Define the scheme, or fix the name.
audit.rule.response-substance.label: Response with neither content nor description
audit.rule.response-substance.message: Response {status} has neither content nor a description.
audit.rule.response-substance.why: It renders as a bare status line: the reader learns that the code exists and nothing else. Describe it, or document what it returns.
audit.rule.version-legacy.label: Superseded spelling in a newer document
audit.rule.version-legacy.message: {construct} is an older spelling, and this document declares OpenAPI {declared}.
audit.rule.version-legacy.why: A reader of the declared version does not know this keyword: it is ignored, and what it carried silently disappears. Write {replacement} instead.
audit.rule.version-construct.label: Construct ahead of the declared version
audit.rule.version-construct.message: {construct} was introduced by OpenAPI {since}, and this document declares {declared}.
audit.rule.version-construct.why: This documentation reads it anyway, but a validator or a code generator trusts the declared version and is entitled to reject the document or drop the construct. Bump the openapi field, or express it with what {declared} offers.
audit.rule.discriminator-mapping.label: Discriminator mapping pointing nowhere
audit.rule.discriminator-mapping.message: The discriminator maps {key} to {target}, which is none of the schemas it can dispatch to.
audit.rule.discriminator-mapping.why: A client reading this mapping cannot tell what shape {key} stands for. This documentation still shows the key, with nothing to expand behind it. Point it at one of the composite's variants, or at a schema that inherits from this one through allOf.
audit.rule.conversion-approximation.mess: collectionFormat: {construct} has no OpenAPI 3.0 equivalent here.
audit.rule.conversion-approximation.why: This document was converted from Swagger {from}, and 3.0 has no style for that delimiter (tsv nowhere, ssv/pipes/multi outside a query parameter). The value is serialized comma-separated instead, so what the try-it sends is not exactly what the document declares. Move the API's contract to a delimiter 3.x defines — csv, ssv, pipes or multi in a query parameter.
audit.rule.schema-dialect.label: Non-default JSON Schema dialect
audit.rule.schema-dialect.why: This documentation reads every schema as JSON Schema 2020-12, whatever the document declares. The keywords the two dialects share behave the same; the ones only your dialect has are read with 2020-12 meaning, or not at all.
audit.rule.operation-described.label: Operation with neither summary nor description
audit.rule.operation-described.message: This operation has neither summary nor description.
audit.rule.operation-described.why: It shows up as a bare method and path, in the page as in the navigation: the reader has to guess what it does from its URL. One summary line is enough.
audit.rule.parameter-described.label: Parameter without description
audit.rule.parameter-described.why: The try-it labels the field with the parameter name and explains it with this description. Without one, the reader gets a box to fill and no idea what belongs in it.
audit.rule.request-body-described.label: Request body without description
audit.rule.request-body-described.messag: The request body has no description.
audit.rule.request-body-described.why: The schema says which fields exist, never which ones go together, what a partial update accepts, or what the API does with them. That belongs in the body's description.
audit.rule.property-described.label: Property without description
audit.rule.property-described.why: The schema view and the body editor show this description next to the field; without one the reader gets a name and a type, and infers the rest.
audit.rule.error-responses-documented.la: Mutating operation with no error response
audit.rule.error-responses-documented.me: This mutating operation documents no error response.
audit.rule.error-responses-documented.wh: Only the happy path is described, while validation, conflict and permission errors are exactly where a consumer needs help. Document at least one 4xx, or a default response.
audit.rule.response-example.label: Response with a schema but no example
audit.rule.response-example.message: Response {status} declares a schema but no example.
audit.rule.response-example.why: The app then shows a sample generated from the schema — structurally right, semantically empty. A hand-written example shows what a real payload looks like.
audit.rule.info-described.label: info.description missing
audit.rule.info-described.why: It is this documentation's home page: without it the reader lands on a title and a list of endpoints, with nothing about what the API is for or how to get access to it.
audit.rule.info-metadata.label: info field missing
audit.rule.info-metadata.why: Who to ask when the API misbehaves, and under what terms it may be used: two fields filled once for the life of the document, and the reader has no other way to find the answers.
audit.rule.link-target.label: Link pointing nowhere
audit.rule.link-target.message: The link {link} points at {target}, which this document declares nowhere.
audit.rule.link-target.why: A link is the API telling the reader which call comes next. Pointing it at an operation the document does not declare breaks the chain it advertises, and the documentation shows the link with nothing to follow. Name an operationId this document declares, or a JSON pointer to one of its operations.
audit.rule.deprecated-inventory.label: Deprecated and still documented
audit.rule.deprecated-inventory.message: Deprecated, and still part of the documented surface.
audit.rule.deprecated-inventory.why: Listed here because no rendered page gathers them: deprecation marks stay wherever they were set. Use the list to plan the removals — or to drop a flag nobody acts on anymore.
audit.rule.deprecation-replacement.label: Deprecation naming no replacement
audit.rule.deprecation-replacement.messa: This deprecation names no replacement and no sunset.
audit.rule.deprecation-replacement.why: The reader learns the thing is going away, not what to do about it. Name the successor in the description, or give a sunset date.
audit.rule.parameter-naming.label: Parameter off the dominant convention
audit.rule.parameter-naming.message: The parameter “{name}” is {style} where the document is mostly {dominant}.
audit.rule.parameter-naming.why: Consumers type these names by hand: a document that mixes conventions turns each of them into a coin flip. Align it with the rest, or accept the mix knowingly.
audit.rule.property-naming.label: Property off the dominant convention
audit.rule.property-naming.message: The property “{name}” is {style} where the document is mostly {dominant}.
audit.rule.property-naming.why: A payload whose keys change convention from one endpoint to the next forces a mapping layer on every consumer — and that layer gets it wrong once.
audit.rule.path-style.label: Path segment off the dominant convention
audit.rule.path-style.message: The segment “{segment}” is {style} where the paths are mostly {dominant}.
audit.rule.path-style.why: URLs are the most public and the least renameable surface of an API: they end up in logs, in bookmarks and in other people's code. A mixed convention costs a lookup on every call.
audit.rule.duplicate-inline-schema.label: Shape written out inline several times
audit.rule.duplicate-inline-schema.messa: This shape is written out inline {count} times.
audit.rule.duplicate-inline-schema.why: The copies are identical today and drift apart the day one of them gets a field. Move it into components.schemas and reference it from each site.
audit.rule.operation-id-present.label: Operation without operationId
audit.rule.operation-id-present.message: No operationId — the deep link falls back to “{fallbackId}”.
audit.rule.operation-id-present.why: That fallback is derived from the method and the path, so every link a reader shares breaks the day the path is renamed. Give the operation a stable operationId.
audit.rule.operation-tagged.label: Operation without tag
audit.rule.operation-tagged.why: It lands in the navigation's catch-all group along with every other untagged operation, and the reader cannot tell which family it belongs to. Give it at least one tag.
audit.rule.servers-declared.label: No server declared
audit.rule.servers-declared.why: Environment seeding has nothing to offer: the reader has to type a base URL by hand before the first try-it call. Declare at least one servers entry.
audit.rule.security-scheme-described.why: The credentials block shows that description to explain what to paste and where to get it. Without one, the reader faces a bare field labelled with the scheme's key.
audit.rule.oauth-flow-urls.label: OAuth flow missing a URL
audit.rule.oauth-flow-urls.why: The try-it runs this flow itself and cannot without that URL: the reader falls back to pasting a token by hand.
audit.rule.operation-examples.label: Operation without any example
audit.rule.operation-examples.message: This operation carries no example, anywhere.
audit.rule.operation-examples.why: The try-it then prefills a sample generated from the schema — valid but meaningless ("string", 0). One hand-written example is what makes the prefilled request sendable as-is.
audit.rule.schema-expand-walls.label: Schema deeper than the auto-expansion
audit.rule.schema-expand-walls.message: Schemas nested deeper than {depth} levels, or recursive.
audit.rule.schema-expand-walls.why: The schema view expands {depth} levels on its own and puts an expand button on everything below. The app handles it, but past that line the structure is only readable click by click.
